task: This is a synthetic writing exercise. Using these fictional reporting notes, write a newspaper reported feature for general readers. Draw only on the supplied notes; do not invent additional reported events, scenes, or quotations. Write from this reporting snapshot as of April 28, 2025. Include a headline. Target 450 to 650 words. Follow AP style.

facts.text: Carmen Delgado, 48, switched 900 of her 1,400 acres in Sandover County to no-till farming in 2020 and enrolled in a voluntary soil carbon program that pays $18 per tonne of carbon sequestered.
After four years, an audit commissioned by the program found Delgado's enrolled fields had sequestered 340 tonnes of carbon — about 40% less than the program's model had projected.
Delgado was paid for 340 tonnes; she accepted the lower figure without dispute but said the gap between the model and the measurement revealed something about how the program was sold.
Delgado said: "They showed me projections of eight hundred tonnes. I signed up for eight hundred tonnes' worth of effort. I got six thousand dollars less than I planned on. That's real money."

The program's auditor, soil consultancy Groundworks Analytics, said the shortfall is not fraud: it reflects the natural variability of soil carbon across a heterogeneous landscape and the tendency of model projections to overestimate in drier-than-average years.

Maria Lindqvist, Groundworks Analytics soil scientist, said: "The model gives an expected value under average conditions. The last four years have not been average. Two of them were drought years. Drought years store less carbon."

Lindqvist said: "The science is right. The communication of uncertainty was not. Projections were presented as targets, not estimates. That gap in framing caused real problems for this farmer and many others."

Delgado said she was not told the projections had wide uncertainty bands: "I read the contract. It said 'estimated based on projected conditions.' I didn't know projected conditions meant 'if it's a normal year, which it may not be.'"

Sandover County has 38 farms enrolled in the same program; preliminary program records show 22 received payouts below their initial projections, 12 received payouts close to projections, and 4 received payouts above projections.

The program administrator, company TerraPay Carbon, said it is revising its farmer communication to present projections as ranges rather than single-point estimates; the revision applies to new enrollments.

A soil carbon policy researcher, Dr. Anita Bauer of Westfield Agricultural Institute, said the Sandover audit results are a useful correction: "Better to find this out at scale in a voluntary program than after mandatory carbon accounting systems are built on the same model assumptions."
Delgado said the no-till transition was worth it for her soil health regardless of the carbon payment: reduced erosion, better water retention, and lower fuel cost from not running tillage equipment.
Delgado said: "I would have switched without the payment. The payment was supposed to make it faster. Instead it made it confusing."

Dr. Bauer said the hardest problem in soil carbon verification is that measurement — physical soil sampling — costs between $300 and $600 per sample location, and credible field-scale estimates require multiple samples: the measurement cost can approach or exceed the payment for small farms.
TerraPay Carbon charges a flat $1,200 audit fee to enrolled farmers; Delgado said she accepted the cost because the program net of audit fees still paid more than she expected when she enrolled.
Lindqvist said the Sandover data will be incorporated into Groundworks' model calibration, which may improve future projections in comparable dryland conditions.
Delgado said she will re-enroll for a second four-year period with the new projection framing: "I know what it means now. It means: if the weather cooperates."

Dr. Bauer said the experience illustrates a tension in voluntary carbon markets: the farmers who most benefit from honest uncertainty framing are precisely the ones who are most likely to be deterred by wide uncertainty bands.
TerraPay Carbon said 78% of Sandover County enrollees said they would re-enroll when surveyed; Delgado was one of them.
Delgado said her final view of the program is complicated: "It works. It just doesn't work the way I thought it did. That's my fault and their fault together."
